## Section 1: Batting Average vs. wRC+
```{r}
library('tidyverse')
library('baseballr')
```
```{r}
# Retrieve 2025 MLB batting statistics
batting_2025 <- fg_batter_leaders(
  startseason = "2025",
  endseason = "2025",
  qual = "200"
)
```

```{r}
head(batting_2025)
```
```{r}
summary(batting_2025)
```
```{r}
dim(batting_2025)
```
```{r}
names(batting_2025)
```

```{r}
glimpse(batting_2025)
```
```{r}
#Ranking Players by wRC+

wrc_leaders <- batting_2025 %>% arrange(desc(wRC_plus)) %>% select(PlayerName, PA, AVG, OBP,
         SLG, HR, wRC_plus) %>% head(10)

wrc_leaders


```

```{r}
# Scatterplot wRC+ vs Avg

ggplot(batting_2025,
       aes(x = AVG, y = wRC_plus)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Does Batting Average Explain Hitting?",
    subtitle = "2025 MLB hitters, minimum 200 PA",
    x = "Batting Average",
    y = "wRC+"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
```{r}
avg_cor <- cor(
  batting_2025$AVG,
  batting_2025$wRC_plus,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

avg_cor
```

```{r}
r_squ_avg <- (avg_cor)^2
r_squ_avg
```

Batting average and wRC+ show a strong positive correlation, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of approximately 0.7314. This suggests that players with higher batting averages tend to have higher wRC+ values. However, this relationship is not surprising, as both statistics are partly based on the same hitting outcomes.

While batting average provides useful information about a hitter's ability to record hits, it does not account for walks or distinguish between singles and extra-base hits. As a result, players with similar batting averages may have substantially different wRC+ values. This suggests that batting average alone may not be enough to evaluate a player's overall offensive performance.

The R-squared value of approximately 0.535 indicates that batting average accounts for 53.5% of the observed variation in wRC+ in our simple linear regression model. This leaves approximately 46.5% of the variation unexplained by the model, suggesting that other offensive statistics may provide additional information about a hitter's performance.

## Section 2: Comparing OBP and Batting Average Using Linear Regression

Research Hypothesis: OBP will have a stronger positive correlation with wRC+ because it accounts for additional ways a hitter can reach base, particularly walks and hit-by-pitches.

*One important consideration: wRC+ itself incorporates the value of reaching base, so we are comparing related measures rather than testing entirely independent characteristics.*

```{r}
obp_cor <- cor(batting_2025$OBP, batting_2025$wRC_plus, use = "complete.obs")
obp_cor
```

```{r}
plot_obp <- ggplot(
  batting_2025,
  aes(x = OBP, y = wRC_plus)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "On-Base Percentage vs wRC+",
    x = "On-Base Percentage",
    y = "wRC+"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot_obp
```
```{r}
r_squ_obp <- obp_cor^2
r_squ_obp
```

```{r}
# Linear regression using batting average
model_avg <- lm(
  wRC_plus ~ AVG,
  data = batting_2025
)

# Linear regression using OBP
model_obp <- lm(wRC_plus ~ OBP, data = batting_2025)

# Compare R-squared values
summary(model_avg)$r.squared
summary(model_obp)$r.squared

```

```{r}
# Compare AVG and OBP
comparison <- tibble(
  Statistic = c("AVG", "OBP"),
  Correlation = c(avg_cor, obp_cor),
  R_squared = c(
    summary(model_avg)$r.squared,
    summary(model_obp)$r.squared
  )
)

print(comparison)
```
Given the data, both batting average (AVG) and on-base percentage (OBP) show strong positive correlations with wRC+. However, OBP has a stronger correlation, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.878 compared to 0.731 for batting average.

Batting average also has a lower R-squared value of 0.535, while OBP has an R-squared value of 0.771. This means that OBP accounts for approximately 77.1% of the observed variation in wRC+ in the simple linear regression model, while batting average accounts for approximately 53.5%.

OBP likely has a stronger relationship with wRC+ because it includes offensive events that batting average does not, such as walks and hit-by-pitches. Alongside hits, these events contribute to a player's ability to reach base and ultimately produce runs, which is reflected in wRC+.

One limitation of this analysis is that OBP and batting average share some of the same underlying components. Additionally, both statistics overlap with the offensive events used to calculate wRC+, meaning that some correlation is expected. While OBP demonstrates a stronger relationship with wRC+ than batting average, it still does not fully capture a hitter's offensive production. In particular, OBP does not distinguish between singles and extra-base hits. This suggests that incorporating a measure of hitting power, such as slugging percentage (SLG), may help explain additional variation in wRC+.
